name: Product manager
summary: Product manager interviews usually test product sense (designing or improving a product for a group of users), analytical thinking (metrics, estimates and diagnosing a change in a number) and how you work with engineers, designers and leaders. Candidates commonly report case-style questions alongside behavioural ones, and for some roles a written exercise or presentation; associate PM interviews often weigh structured thinking more than past experience.
rounds: Product sense round: design or improve a product for a group of users
Analytical round: metrics, estimates and diagnosing a drop in a number
Execution or technical round: prioritising, trade-offs and working with engineers
Behavioural or leadership round, often with a senior product leader
Written exercise or presentation for some roles
looks_for: Starting from users and their problems before features
Structured thinking that's easy to follow
Metrics that reflect real value, with guardrails
Prioritising with clear reasons, and saying no
Influencing engineering, design and business without formal authority
Comfort with data, and enough technical understanding to discuss trade-offs

questions.text: Tell me about a product or feature you launched. How did you decide what to build?
covers: The user problem, and how you knew it was worth solving
How you chose the solution and what you left out
The result against the metric you set beforehand

questions.text: Describe a time you had to say no to a senior stakeholder's request.
covers: The request, and why it didn't fit the priorities
How you explained it with data or user evidence
What you offered instead, and how the relationship held up

questions.text: Tell me about a launch that didn't go as planned.
covers: What you expected and what actually happened
How you responded in the first few days
What you changed about how you plan or test launches

questions.text: Tell me about a time engineering and design disagreed about a feature. How did you help them decide?
covers: The two views and the trade-off behind them
How you brought the discussion back to users and goals
The decision, and how you kept everyone committed to it

questions.text: Pick an app you use every day. Who is it for, and what one change would you make?
covers: Its main user groups, and the one you'd focus on
A specific problem, how you know it exists, and your change
How you'd measure whether the change worked

questions.text: Design a product that helps older people manage their medicines.
covers: Clarifying who exactly: the person, a carer, a family member, a pharmacist
The key problems: remembering doses, refills, mixing up medicines
A simple first version, what you'd leave out, and how you'd test it

questions.text: Weekly active users of a feature dropped 10% this week. How would you find out why?
covers: Ruling out tracking bugs, releases, holidays and seasonality first
Splitting the drop by platform, region, user type and step in the flow
The most likely cause, how you'd confirm it, and what you'd do next

questions.text: How would you measure the success of a new messaging feature in a social app?
covers: The goal of the feature, then one main metric tied to it
Supporting and guardrail metrics, such as spam reports or replies per conversation
How you'd notice if it helped one group of users and hurt another

questions.text: Estimate how many people in Bengaluru use a ride-hailing app on a typical weekday. Talk me through your reasoning.
covers: A clear structure: population, share who travel daily, share using ride-hailing
Stated, sensible assumptions with round numbers
A quick sanity check on the final figure

questions.text: You have five requested features and capacity for two this quarter. How do you choose?
covers: Tying each feature to goals and to user impact
Estimating effort and risk with engineering
A simple framework such as impact versus effort or RICE, and explaining the choice to those who lose out

questions.text: What goes into a good product requirements document for a new feature?
covers: The problem, the users and the goals
Scope, what's explicitly out of scope, and success metrics
Open questions and risks, and how design and engineering shape the document

questions.text: How do you decide whether to run an A/B test or simply launch a change?
covers: Risk, how easy it is to reverse, and whether there are enough users for a test
What you'd measure and for how long
When user research or a staged rollout is enough

questions.text: Users say the app feels slow. How would you work with engineers to understand and fix it?
covers: A basic picture of where time goes: device, network, server, database
Asking for measurements and agreeing a target
Weighing speed work against features, with user impact as the reason

questions.text: A competitor has just launched a feature our users keep asking for. What do you do?
covers: Understanding why users want it, and how many
Whether it fits your strategy, rather than copying by reflex
Options: build it, build something different, or not build it, and how you'd test the choice

questions.text: How would you talk to users to decide what to build next?
covers: Finding the right users and asking about past behaviour, not wishes about the future
Avoiding leading questions
Combining what they say with what usage data shows

questions.text: Why product management, and why now?
covers: Experiences that drew you to it: a project, a launch, a problem you owned
Skills you bring from your background
What you most want to learn as a PM

questions.text: Which part of our product do you think could be better, and what would you change first?
covers: Evidence that you've used the product properly
A specific problem and a focused change
The metric that would tell you it worked

tips: In product questions, say who the user is and what problem you're solving before naming any feature.
State your structure at the start (users, problems, solutions, metrics) so the interviewer can follow and redirect you.
Finish with a clear recommendation; a balanced list with no choice is a common weak spot.
Use the company's product properly before the interview and note specific details, not general impressions.
For associate PM roles, show product thinking through college projects, internships or things you've built yourself.
Keep estimates simple: round numbers, stated assumptions and a quick sanity check.
